cards.title: Mine competitor video transcripts with an LLM for ad angles
cards.summary: Feed a proven creator's video transcripts into an LLM and prompt it for angles, stories, common phrases and audience-relatability hooks to speed up copy research.
cards.use_when: You need ad angles, email hooks or landing-page copy for a product in an unfamiliar category and want to absorb a proven creator's messaging before writing.
steps: Pick 3-5 videos from a person who already sells successfully to your target buyer. Open each video, use the transcript feature (interface changes—verify current steps), copy the full transcript, and paste all of them into an LLM along with a labeling instruction like 'These are transcripts of how this person talks and what they say.'
Request the specific outputs you need: angles that justify a claim, story ideas, and copy blocks.

For a single video, ask the model to: distill it into a few paragraphs of the most important points; list common phrases used; identify the core message; describe any stories (what happened, who was involved); and flag places where the speaker relates to the audience by showing they understand what the audience thinks and why.
Seed your ad or email copy with the mined hooks, sayings and offer logic, substituting your product's specifics.
A ~17-minute video can be summarized in about 30 seconds this way, making research efficient.
caveats: Reuse ideas and structure, not the exact words—high-input research with low-output copy wastes time.
The LLM output is only as good as the transcripts; verify the niche, offer and audience yourself.

cards.title: Segment subscribers by how they joined before emailing them
cards.summary: Segment email subscribers by acquisition source—newsletter opt-in, free lead magnet, or past buyer—because each group expects different content and offers.
cards.use_when: You are planning an email sequence, welcome flow or promotion for a store and need to decide which message each segment receives.
steps: List every way someone can join your list: a newsletter opt-in seeking entertainment or exclusivity, a free lead magnet traded for a specific download or tool, and previous buyers who already trusted you enough to pay.

For each source, write down what the subscriber expects: newsletter subscribers want exclusive insights and updates; lead-magnet subscribers want the promised specific outcome; customers want more of what they bought plus complementary products.

Match the offer and angle to the segment. Do not send a hard sales email to newsletter subscribers who signed up for entertainment, and do not send generic nurture to buyers ready for the next-step offer.
If you run different lead magnets or launch offers, keep separate sequences per offer instead of one blended list.
caveats: Source-specific example: a real-estate creator's newsletter subscribers opted in for exclusive insights, so emails sold more insights rather than a cold pitch.
This is a structural framework from the source's experience, not a tested benchmark; adapt to your own list.

cards.title: Build a prospect profile document from a brand's own content
cards.summary: Compile a creator's or brand's captions, hooks, sayings, angles, offer and stories into one document so your ad, email and PDP copy matches their voice and logic.
cards.use_when: You are writing ads, emails or landing pages for a brand or creator whose voice and offer you need to absorb quickly.
steps: Create a single document and paste in several social captions plus transcripts of a few videos.

Write down what the offer actually is in plain terms. You cannot write about an offer you don't understand—the source had to learn that flex space means office warehouses rented to offices, warehouses, retail or restaurants.
Add a section for hooks: copy the exact opening lines that made you stop scrolling.
Add a section for common sayings and recurring phrases that sound like the person.
Add a section for angles and justifications: the arguments they repeatedly use to make their offer the obvious choice.
Add a section for stories: what happened, who was involved, how it resolved—with a main takeaway lesson at the end.

Add a section for audience relatability: lines proving the speaker understands what the audience thinks and why. Example from a real-estate reel: 'if you're done with problematic tenants and 2 a.m. maintenance calls, I get it.'
Use this profile as the source of truth when drafting copy so the output matches their voice and logic rather than generic marketing language.
caveats: The document is a research asset, not a script—steal ideas and structure, not exact words.
The source demonstrates this on a real-estate creator; verify offer details yourself rather than assuming.

cards.title: Write a first marketing email as a story with a delayed reveal
cards.summary: Structure a promo email by stating the problem, hinting at the solution, deepening the pain, describing your own experience, then revealing the product and giving one CTA.
cards.use_when: You need to write a promotional email that moves readers from problem awareness to a click without sounding like an ad.
steps: Open with a hook tied to the reader's current pain: 'Why I sold my residential properties and after hearing this you might too.'

Relate to desired outcomes (freedom, passive income, tax benefits) and then challenge them: 'I soon came to realize real estate provides almost none of those things—at least if you follow how everyone else does it or teaches it.'
Deepen the problem with concrete pain points a real buyer recognizes: 2 a.m. calls to fix broken toilets, tenants avoiding rent, the stress of finding deals.

Describe your own experience with the solution without naming it: 'I tried something new and instantly it was like a breath of fresh air.' Stay intriguing—don't reveal the answer in the next sentence.
Reveal what it is only after describing your experience and why it's better, flipping the common order of naming the product first and praising it after.
End with one clear CTA and offer: 'if you want to learn how, click here to join.'
Add situational urgency only where true, e.g. the opportunity likely won't be as accessible to beginners in a few years.
caveats: The source's example sells a program at over seven figures per development—results are the source's anecdote, not a guarantee for your product.
Delaying the reveal only works if the payoff delivers real value; otherwise it reads as clickbait.

cards.title: Show your own conviction instead of telling readers they should buy
cards.summary: Persuasion friction drops when you demonstrate your own conviction and reasoning rather than repeatedly telling people they should buy.
cards.use_when: You are writing ad copy, emails or a sales page and catch yourself using pressure language like 'you need to get in before it's too late.'
steps: Replace imperative claims with personal conviction: instead of 'you need to get into X before it's too late,' write why you yourself went all in while the opportunity was there.
Add a reflective regret frame: name opportunities you watched pass by while others profited and you stayed on the sidelines, giving the reader a concrete emotional picture without attacking them.
Tie the conviction to real, checkable reasoning—specific benefits, timing or mechanics you genuinely believe in.
Use the conviction to create situational urgency: real constraints like 'when I got in the opportunity was still there, but maybe not forever,' rather than manufactured deadlines.
Keep the tone like a friend talking to a friend—short and punchy, not an exam paper.
caveats: Conviction framing is the source's opinion and technique; it is not a universal rule that pressure never works.
Situational urgency must be genuine, or it becomes the same clickbait problem it is meant to avoid.

cards.title: Score every asset against the four-part copy formula
cards.summary: Every piece of copy—email, ad, sales page—needs attention, consumption, persuasion and action, and the beginning deserves the most effort.
cards.use_when: You are drafting, reviewing or diagnosing any ad, email, landing page or VSL and need a checklist for what might be missing.
steps: Attention: get past the brain's 'spam filter.' Write the hook or headline first and spend disproportionate time on it—successful creators spend most effort on title, thumbnail and first seconds because nothing else matters if the reader never starts.
Consumption: make the copy easy and intriguing to read. If it isn't consumable, message quality is irrelevant.
Persuasion: shift the reader's beliefs in your favor—this is how selling works over time.
Action: end with an effective call to action.

When an asset underperforms, score it against these four; the weakest stage is usually the one to rewrite. A strong hook leaves no wasted words—the source's example is a short scenario hook that creates immediate curiosity.
caveats: The four-part formula is a rule of thumb from the source, not a guaranteed conversion driver.
Attention-getting hooks that don't lead to consumable, value-delivering copy break at stages two and three.

cards.title: Make a promise, not spam: lower reading effort and raise intrigue
cards.summary: Grab attention by decreasing the effort required to read while increasing intrigue; promises must be exciting but not spammy or platform-noncompliant.
cards.use_when: You are writing ad hooks, email subject lines or landing-page headlines and need to be exciting without triggering spam filters or ad rejections.
steps: Lower consumption effort: write lean, short, punchy copy without fluff. Long intros that bury the point get abandoned.
Raise intrigue: give hints the reader cannot guess—like a guessing game ('guess what we're eating today,' then 'it starts with an m'), where each wrong guess increases investment.

Make a promise that isn't spammy. Instead of 'make $10,000 in 20 days $$$,' write an exciting specific benefit the reader gets if they read on. Spammy wording can send email to the spam folder—the source cites open rates dropping from 25-30% to about 5% or less when messages land in spam.
Stay platform-compliant. Meta and Gmail enforce content rules; copy that even looks spammy can get an ad account shut down. Be honest like you're talking to a friend.
Add emotion without clickbait: use high-tension, surprising moments but always tie the payoff to real value so readers don't feel cheated.
caveats: The open-rate figures (25-30% vs 5%) are the source's illustrative numbers, not a controlled benchmark.
Platform rules change—verify current Gmail and Meta advertising policies before relying on claims.

cards.title: Use the three-part attention formula: promise, intrigue, emotion
cards.summary: Grab reader attention by combining a non-spammy promise, non-confusing intrigue and emotional drama with a real payoff instead of clickbait.
cards.use_when: You are crafting hooks for social ads, email subject lines or opening paragraphs and need them to stop the scroll.
steps: Promise (not spammy): tell readers something amazing they will get if they keep reading—'this is the coolest game ever, you can fly around and fight dragons' rather than just 'it's fun.' Keep claims honest enough to be compliant.

Intrigue (not confusing): make readers curious without confusing them. Confusion kills reading—avoid over-technical language even when writing to smart business owners, because easy-to-digest messages reach both weaker and stronger readers.

Build intrigue in steps: 'double your Instagram followers in 4 months without spending a dime—here's how I did it. First you need the power of engaging content—but not just any content. There's a special type of post that gets 7-10 times more engagement than regular posts. No, it's not reels, carousels or single photos.' Then end with payoff and a click.

Emotion (not clickbait): use dramatic hooks and suspense—'I'm quitting copywriting and starting drop shipping—here's why'—build suspense ('I've heard beginners say this over and over'), then reveal the twist.
Verify the emotional promise matches the content. Clickbait is a subject line or thumbnail that doesn't match what's inside—even if value exists, readers feel cheated.
Contrarian framing: challenge a commonly held belief (the source calls this the 'big challenge') to generate interest from people who want to know why you disagree.
caveats: The 7-10x engagement figure is the source's claim about a specific post type, not a general benchmark.
Contrarian disagreement draws attention but risks alienating the audience if the position isn't backed by real reasoning or value.

cards.title: Write for short attention spans by maximizing value per minute
cards.summary: Value value-per-minute over total value, using short sentences, bullets, visuals and a direct CTA.
cards.use_when: You are writing emails, PDP copy, ad creative or landing pages for an audience that scrolls short-form content.
steps: Judge copy by value delivered per minute, not total volume—a 200-word email with high value beats a 10,000-word email stuffed with value, because nobody reads the long one.
Start with a strong hook: 'Add 2 inches to your biceps in just 90 days—here's how' is specific about who and what; 'grow your arms' is vague and not fresh.
Use short sentences and paragraphs to stay simple and direct.
Use bullets and lists to pack maximum value into the most scannable format—e.g. 'lift heavy weights; eat 1g of protein per pound of body weight daily; get eight hours of sleep each night.'
Use visuals sparingly: one or two emojis in an email, more allowed in a caption, to convey emotion or point attention to your single biggest lesson.
Be direct—skip fluff and tell readers exactly what to do, like 'consume a protein shake within 30 minutes after your workout.'
End with a clear call to action, e.g. 'download the free 90-day arm building plan.'
caveats: The 200 vs 10,000-word comparison is the source's illustration, not a measured outcome.
Emoji and visual density should fit the channel—overloading an email with emojis looks unprofessional.

cards.title: Vary pacing like an action movie to hold attention
cards.summary: Alternate slow, explanatory passages with short, fast, exciting lines so copy has natural rhythm instead of being all slow or all fast.
cards.use_when: You are editing an email, sales page or VSL script that feels flat, chunky or exhausting to read.
steps: Recognize the two failure modes: all fast (nothing but fight scenes gets boring) and all slow (exposition with no action gets boring). Good copy alternates, like a roller coaster.

Slow down to explain when you need clarity: use longer sentences and more detail for the core teaching—e.g. 'To build muscle effectively you need to understand the role of protein in muscle repair and growth.'
Don't over-explain. Avoid diving into protein synthesis and ratios—that reads like a study and bores readers. Sprinkle small short items (bullets) within explanations to keep pace.
Speed up to excite with short punchy sentences—e.g. a recap: 'Lift heavy. Eat right. Sleep well. Watch your muscles grow.'
Mix it up: alternate slow and fast cadences for natural flow—e.g. 'Building muscle isn't just about lifting weights—it's about strategy. Random lifting wastes time.'
Use transitional phrases to move smoothly between paces, e.g. 'now that you know the basics, let's get to the fun part.'

Avoid long blocks of text at the top followed by short lines at the bottom—that kills pacing. Spaced, uneven line lengths read more easily than big chunky paragraphs, which look like a book people don't want to read.
caveats: Pacing advice is a stylistic principle from the source, not a tested conversion lift.
Examples use fitness copy—substitute your own vertical's language.

cards.title: Shift limiting beliefs before pitching the offer
cards.summary: People already know what to do; their limiting beliefs stop them—prove you understand the belief, disprove it, install the new belief, then sell using it.
cards.use_when: You are writing a sales page, VSL or email and the audience resists buying despite knowing the general solution exists.
steps: Identify the desire and the limiting belief blocking it. Desires like 'lose weight and get in shape' are blocked by beliefs like 'healthy food is expensive,' 'I'm big boned,' 'my genetics are bad,' 'I'm too busy.'

Write value at the 'how' level, not the 'what' level. 'Eat less, burn more, go to the gym consistently' is something people already know, so it isn't valuable. Write 'how to curb cravings,' 'how fasting helps you eat less while staying full,' 'the best routine to do at the gym,' 'how to stay consistent.'

Follow the belief-shift sequence: (1) state the limiting belief in the reader's own words—'I can't lose weight because I hate being hungry'; (2) challenge it—'starving yourself and being hungry all the time isn't the answer'; (3) sympathize—'most people are told fewer calories equals less weight, but they've been lied to'; (4) disprove the old belief with a concrete failure mode—hunger leads to binge cycles and is terrible for weight loss; (5) install the new belief—'losing weight is about strategic ways to stay full throughout the day while eating fewer calories'; (6) sell from the new belief—'if you want a meal plan built around your time and taste preferences, click here.'

Support the new belief with proof—the source pairs the claim with side-by-side meal comparisons (a homemade stuffed-crust pizza at 900 calories and 80g protein versus fast food with more calories, less protein and triple the fat).
caveats: The nutrition macro figures are illustrations from the source's example, not verified data—verify any such claims before using them in your copy.
Correcting people directly ('1+1=3, wrong') causes friction and defensiveness; understanding framing ('I see how you could think that—I thought so too until...') is more effective.

cards.title: Submit evidence strong enough that belief follows
cards.summary: You cannot force belief by demanding it; supply evidence strong enough that holding the belief becomes difficult, using analogies, quotes, statistics, cost narration, hypotheticals and borrowed authority.
cards.use_when: You are writing a sales page, VSL or ad that asks the reader to change how they see a product category or accept a claim they may doubt.
steps: Use analogies to map the unfamiliar onto the familiar: 'a computer is like a brain because it processes information.' Apply the same to your mechanism or offer.
Use quotes to provide authoritative support and emotional resonance for an idea, raising credibility.
Use statistics to give concrete, factual evidence supporting your claim and building trust. Verify any statistic before publishing.

Use cost narration to demonstrate the significant effort or investment behind your claim or knowledge—it shows value and credibility. Example: explain how much research or iteration went into your method or product.
Use hypothetical examples to show how your concept plays out in real-life situations, making outcomes visual and relatable.
Use borrowed authority, like quotes, to leverage the credibility of experts or respected sources and transfer trust to your argument.

The framing exercise: you can't truly choose a belief without evidence. A kidnapper demanding you believe he's Jesus won't work—but if he turns water to wine, walks on water and splits the sea, belief becomes almost unavoidable. Write copy that supplies that level of evidence for your claim.
caveats: This is a persuasion philosophy from the source, not a measured framework.
Manufacturing false proof or unverified statistics violates the honest-promise principle and can breach ad platform rules.
